newsitem.title: BELARUS: Sacked electoral chief says Belarus vote faked.
newsitem.headline: Sacked electoral chief says Belarus vote faked.

text.p: Opposition figures in Belarus, including a top electoral official sacked by hardline President Alexander Lukashenko, cast doubt on the validity of a referendum whose results on Monday gave him a huge majority.
Viktor Gonchar, elected by parliament but dismissed days before Sunday's vote which he declared invalid in advance, said the high turnout figure of 84 percent had clearly been faked.
"Even during the presidential campaign (in 1994), when political activity was at its highest, it was lower. The figures are simply fantastic," he said.
In a telephone interview early on Monday, Gonchar focussed particularly on a big jump in turnout in the evening.
The percentage of the electorate which had voted jumped by 26 points between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m., and Gonchar said it had only increased by seven to nine points at previous polls.
Lukashenko told a news conference later on Monday that the late flood of voters resulted from people returning to towns after weekend trips to countryside homes and vegetable plots.
"Most town dwellers voted after they returned from their dachas," he said.

Semyon Sharetsky, the main opposition figure who heads a majority of deputies in parliament seeking to remove Lukashenko from office, ridiculed the notion that so many voters would have been tending their gardens in late November.

"It was cold, dark and slushy. This is suspicious," he told a news conference after results showed more than 70 percent of the electorate had backed Lukashenko's constitutional draft to give him extra powers.

Controversy has also arisen around the financing of the referendum, which included a question proposed by parliament on banning off-budget funds which was rejected by more than two thirds of the electorate.

Deputies have accused Lukashenko of siphoning off state funds to finance his campaign, during which he sent postcards of his smiling face to the entire electorate, invitations to take part in advance voting which began on November 9 and monopolised state television and radio.
"It is not really very good to look in someone else's pocket," Lukashenko said, adding that the campaign cost up to 17 billion Belarussian roubles -- about $850,000.
"Most of the contributions came from voluntary donations by citizens and enterprises," he said. The average salary in the former Soviet republic is about $50 a month.
Western bodies including the U.S. congress, the European Union and the Council of Europe decided not to send official observers, fearing they would appear to be validating the poll.
Lukashenko ignored the existing constitution and overruled decisions against him by the constitutional court and parliament in order to push through his referendum.
A five-member European parliament delegation did come to Minsk at the invitation of Sharetsky to monitor the overnight count, though it did not seek accreditation in advance.
Its leader Herbert Bosch told Reuters it had not been allowed to watch the ballot papers being counted.
"We saw some irregularities yesterday, but the question is whether the whole procedure is regular or not," he said.
Electoral official Georgy Pashkovsky was infuriated when asked by telephone how much access observers had had.

"You, a solid news agency, you think we are not a democratic country, a civilised society? Observers were allowed to watch the voting and the count," he exclaimed, adding: "But they cannot replace the electoral commissions."
And Lukashenko declared the vote was flawless.

"The referendum, according to my information, ran like clockwork...We invited foreign observers here, and in this way the referendum was recognised. Such a big number of journalists says a lot too," he declared before the world's mass media.
Asked if the West would fail to recognise the results as a way of putting pressure on him to fall in line with its idea of reforms, Lukashenko was nonchalant.
"I'm not scared of pressure. If they pressurise me, that will be their problem. It's a bit late to put pressure on me," he said. "And what's more, to crush me, that's impossible."
The election was seen as a foregone conclusion, all the more so since state television ran daily slots showing how to vote for Lukashenko, and against parliament.

Lukashenko's aggressive campaign ran throughout the two-week period of advance voting, which according to a parliament decision should only have been intended for those who could not turn up on November 24.
"This election was decided before it began," the head of the International Helsinki Federation in Vienna, Aaron Rhodes, said by telephone.
Bosch of the European parliament said: "I do not understand why Russia only needs one day to carry out a referendum while little Belarus needs two weeks."
